# Access management

**Website sign-in.** Slack-authenticated access links redirect the account owner
to Kernel Managed Auth's hosted login. Kernel discovers the login flow, collects
passwords and fresh SMS/email codes, and saves a successful authenticated profile.
Clanker resumes the original task only after this exact flow reports success.
Pending flows are reused without restarting; failures are not automatically
retried. First migration sign-in may require credentials again: write-only Vault
passwords cannot be imported into Managed Auth through a documented bridge.
Use `clanker_authenticate`; the old login-fill/code tools are compatibility aliases.

**Collection and storage.** Kernel Vault continues to store personal details and
API keys. Existing Vault login items remain protected. Clanker's local database keeps
ownership, opaque handles, consent, request status and fill claims. Its former
credential forms and encrypted credential writers are disabled. A protected
encrypted migration archive is retained outside active profiles for recovery.

**Use and reuse.** Clanker receives credential handles and metadata. A handle is
an ID, such as `vault_a1b2c3d4e5f6`, pointing to a saved credential. It contains no
secret and does not grant access by itself. The backend checks the requester's
permission before starting Managed Auth. Passwords, codes and authenticator seeds
are not returned to Clanker. API keys use the separately approved backend read
path below and stay out of model arguments. Each requester, account and task
gets an isolated Kernel auth profile. Automation loads its successful snapshot
with `save_changes: false`; it never copies cookies or writes back to the profile.
Stopping the task deletes its remote browser, connection and profile with absence
checks. A later task can reference the Kernel-managed saved credential in a fresh
isolated profile. SMS/email verification always needs a fresh interactive code.
Cookies alone do not
authorize using an account; Clanker requires owned or explicitly invited access.

**Personal details.** Names, addresses, phone numbers, email and dates of birth
are model-blind by default. An owner can explicitly allow Clanker's model to read
only the saved primary fields required for a private task and adapt them to the
website's actual form. This consent is owner-scoped; it does not expose invited
accounts, gender, passwords, cards, tokens or verification codes. Public Slack
updates still redact personal values. Authorized reads can persist in private
model conversation history; revocation stops future reads without erasing data
already seen. Kernel stores ordinary details as non-sensitive fields so the
trusted backend can format them for a website; gender remains opaque. The model
consent check is separate from that backend access. See [the consent policy](decisions/2026-10-08-consented-personal-model-access.md).

**Private continuation.** A task can move from a shared Slack thread to the
owner's DM while retaining its context internally. Private questions, values and
ordinary replies stay there. Shared-thread updates identify the intended member
and contain meaningful public milestones or the verified outcome, not copied DM
dialogue.

**Sharing.** Owners invite a Slack member to use selected credentials. Invitations
grant neither the whole vault nor onward sharing, and newly saved credentials are
not automatically included. Managed Auth grants use a separate recipient/task
profile and a saved Kernel credential reference. Legacy Vault credentials must
have a dedicated Kernel vault; recipients never attach the owner's general vault. The migration preserves
the existing shared login in a dedicated vault. New invitations for credentials
in a general vault are refused until an isolated mapping is provisioned.
Membership and grants are checked at use time.
Sharing a login inherits that website account's permissions; it does not create
read-only access. Automatic payment submission and card/CVV collection are
unavailable. Clanker prepares the cart in Kernel and stops before purchase
commitment so the owner can complete checkout personally.

**API integrations.** The owner approved storing API keys as Kernel credential
fields with `type: "text"` and `sensitive: false`. This setting makes the value
readable through authenticated Kernel item responses; it does not make the key
public. Kernel remains the credential store. Clanker keeps only ownership,
opaque handles and execution claims locally, with no active local key copy.

The scoped `clanker_api_request` tool accepts an opaque handle and a JSON request.
The trusted backend checks owned or explicitly invited access and the credential's
exact HTTPS API origin, then injects authentication for that request. Keys do not
enter model context, tool arguments, generated scripts, shell environments or
logs. Code tasks use this tool for authenticated requests instead of receiving a
raw key. Passwords and TOTP seeds retain their opaque, sensitive representation.

Existing sensitive API-key fields cannot be exported or changed to readable
fields because Kernel field types and sensitivity are immutable. They require
a replacement item and private recollection or import from an independently
available source. The reviewed live inventory contained no saved API-key items,
so this rollout needs no recollection. API execution is being restored; a passing
local check does not establish acceptance by a live API provider. See
[the approved execution boundary](decisions/2026-10-08-kernel-api-key-execution.md).

**Revocation.** Revoking an invitation denies further credential use and cancels
pending handoffs. If it was used in a browser, the recipient's affected context
stays blocked until cleanup succeeds. Kernel cleanup requires confirmed remote
browser deletion followed by an API response showing that session is absent.
Uncertain cleanup stays recorded and blocks reuse. Deleting a browser is not
merchant-side logout or revocation of the underlying website account.

**Trust and limits.** Kernel hosts the browser and therefore receives entered
website secrets and page content. The adapter verifies requester ownership,
remote session identity, exact authenticated profile and origin before private fills;
attachment to another requester's general vault is disabled. Kernel
fill can emit untrusted input events. Provider success and nonempty DOM controls
do not establish website acceptance: observe the actual login or checkout state.
Managed Auth transport and profile handoff are tested separately from real
merchant login and SMS verification, which still require user participation.
Encryption does not protect
against a compromised host or browser provider. These controls need continuing
live acceptance evidence and do not create narrower permissions inside a shared
website account. Historical Composio records do not represent an active browser
connection or prove deletion of old provider resources.

# Access management

**Website sign-in.** Slack-authenticated access links redirect the account owner
to Kernel Managed Auth's hosted login. Kernel discovers the login flow, collects
passwords and fresh SMS/email codes, and saves a successful authenticated profile.
Clanker resumes the original task only after this exact flow reports success.
Pending flows are reused without restarting; failures are not automatically
retried. First migration sign-in may require credentials again: write-only Vault
passwords cannot be imported into Managed Auth through a documented bridge.
Use `clanker_authenticate`; the old login-fill/code tools are compatibility aliases.

**Collection and storage.** Kernel Vault continues to store personal details and
API keys. Existing Vault login items remain protected. Clanker's local database keeps
ownership, opaque handles, consent, request status and fill claims. Its former
credential forms and encrypted credential writers are disabled. A protected
encrypted migration archive is retained outside active profiles for recovery.

**Use and reuse.** Clanker receives credential handles and metadata. A handle is
an ID, such as `vault_a1b2c3d4e5f6`, pointing to a saved credential. It contains no
secret and does not grant access by itself. The backend checks the requester's
permission before starting Managed Auth. Passwords, codes and authenticator seeds
are not returned to Clanker. API keys use the separately approved backend read
path below and stay out of model arguments. Each requester, account and task
gets an isolated Kernel auth profile. Automation loads its successful snapshot
with `save_changes: false`; it never copies cookies or writes back to the profile.
Stopping the task deletes its remote browser, connection and profile with absence
checks. A later task can reference the Kernel-managed saved credential in a fresh
isolated profile. SMS/email verification always needs a fresh interactive code.
Cookies alone do not
authorize using an account; Clanker requires owned or explicitly invited access.

**Personal details.** Names, addresses, phone numbers, email and dates of birth
are model-blind by default. An owner can explicitly allow Clanker's model to read
only the saved primary fields required for a private task and adapt them to the
website's actual form. This consent is owner-scoped; it does not expose invited
accounts, gender, passwords, cards, tokens or verification codes. Public Slack
updates still redact personal values. Authorized reads can persist in private
model conversation history; revocation stops future reads without erasing data
already seen. Kernel stores ordinary details as non-sensitive fields so the
trusted backend can format them for a website; gender remains opaque. The model
consent check is separate from that backend access. See [the consent policy](decisions/2026-10-08-consented-personal-model-access.md).

**Private continuation.** A task can move from a shared Slack thread to the
owner's DM while retaining its context internally. Private questions, values and
ordinary replies stay there. Shared-thread updates identify the intended member
and contain meaningful public milestones or the verified outcome, not copied DM
dialogue.

**Sharing.** Owners invite a Slack member to use selected credentials. Invitations
grant neither the whole vault nor onward sharing, and newly saved credentials are
not automatically included. Managed Auth grants use a separate recipient/task
profile and a saved Kernel credential reference. Legacy Vault credentials must
have a dedicated Kernel vault; recipients never attach the owner's general vault. The migration preserves
the existing shared login in a dedicated vault. New invitations for credentials
in a general vault are refused until an isolated mapping is provisioned.
Membership and grants are checked at use time.
Sharing a login inherits that website account's permissions; it does not create
read-only access. Automatic payment submission and card/CVV collection are
unavailable. Clanker prepares the cart in Kernel and stops before purchase
commitment so the owner can complete checkout personally.

**API integrations.** The owner approved storing API keys as Kernel credential
fields with `type: "text"` and `sensitive: false`. This setting makes the value
readable through authenticated Kernel item responses; it does not make the key
public. Kernel remains the credential store. Clanker keeps only ownership,
opaque handles and execution claims locally, with no active local key copy.

The scoped `clanker_api_request` tool accepts an opaque handle and a JSON request.
The trusted backend checks owned or explicitly invited access and the credential's
exact HTTPS API origin, then injects authentication for that request. Keys do not
enter model context, tool arguments, generated scripts, shell environments or
logs. Code tasks use this tool for authenticated requests instead of receiving a
raw key. Passwords and TOTP seeds retain their opaque, sensitive representation.

Existing sensitive API-key fields cannot be exported or changed to readable
fields because Kernel field types and sensitivity are immutable. They require
a replacement item and private recollection or import from an independently
available source. The reviewed live inventory contained no saved API-key items,
so this rollout needs no recollection. API execution is being restored; a passing
local check does not establish acceptance by a live API provider. See
[the approved execution boundary](decisions/2026-10-08-kernel-api-key-execution.md).

**Revocation.** Revoking an invitation denies further credential use and cancels
pending handoffs. If it was used in a browser, the recipient's affected context
stays blocked until cleanup succeeds. Kernel cleanup requires confirmed remote
browser deletion followed by an API response showing that session is absent.
Uncertain cleanup stays recorded and blocks reuse. Deleting a browser is not
merchant-side logout or revocation of the underlying website account.

**Trust and limits.** Kernel hosts the browser and therefore receives entered
website secrets and page content. The adapter verifies requester ownership,
remote session identity, exact authenticated profile and origin before private fills;
attachment to another requester's general vault is disabled. Kernel
fill can emit untrusted input events. Provider success and nonempty DOM controls
do not establish website acceptance: observe the actual login or checkout state.
Managed Auth transport and profile handoff are tested separately from real
merchant login and SMS verification, which still require user participation.
Encryption does not protect
against a compromised host or browser provider. These controls need continuing
live acceptance evidence and do not create narrower permissions inside a shared
website account. Historical Composio records do not represent an active browser
connection or prove deletion of old provider resources.

#   scripts/run_tests.sh -j 4                       # cap parallelism
#   scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/               # discover only here
#   scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/ tests/acp_adapter/    # multiple roots
#   scripts/run_tests.sh tests/foo.py               # single file
#   scripts/run_tests.sh tests/foo.py -q            # path + bare pytest flag
#   scripts/run_tests.sh tests/foo.py -v --tb=long  # bare flags "just work"
#   scripts/run_tests.sh -k 'pattern'               # value flags pass through too

# bare flags. Positional path arguments override the default discovery
# root (tests/).

set -euo pipefail

# ── Locate repo root ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"

# ── Locate python ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Probe local venvs first; fall back to the Nix devShell's editable venv
# (HERMES_PYTHON is exported by the devShell hook and ships [dev] extras:
# pytest, pytest-asyncio, pytest-timeout, ruff, ty).
#
# A candidate must have pytest INSTALLED, not merely exist. The release venv
# at ~/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv has bin/activate but no pytest, so an
# existence-only probe selected it in checkouts/worktrees without a local
# .venv — every file then died with "No module named pytest" and the run
# reported "0 tests passed" (which reads green at a glance even though the
# exit code is 1). Skip such a venv and keep probing instead.
VENV=""
VENV_PYTHON=""
SKIPPED_VENVS=""
for candidate in "$REPO_ROOT/.venv" "$REPO_ROOT/venv" "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv"; do
  if [ -f "$candidate/bin/activate" ]; then
    if "$candidate/bin/python" -c 'import pytest' 2>/dev/null; then
      VENV="$candidate"
      VENV_PYTHON="$candidate/bin/python"
      break
    fi
    SKIPPED_VENVS="$SKIPPED_VENVS $candidate"
  fi
  # Native Windows venv layout: python.exe and activate live under
  # Scripts/, and there is no bin/. Anyone running this script from
  # Git Bash / MSYS with a `python -m venv`- or uv-created venv hits
  # this branch — without it the canonical runner refuses to start.
  if [ -f "$candidate/Scripts/activate" ]; then
    if "$candidate/Scripts/python.exe" -c 'import pytest' 2>/dev/null; then
      VENV="$candidate"
      VENV_PYTHON="$candidate/Scripts/python.exe"
      break
    fi
    SKIPPED_VENVS="$SKIPPED_VENVS $candidate"
  fi
done

  for skipped in $SKIPPED_VENVS; do
    echo "▶ skipping venv without pytest: $skipped" >&2
  done
fi

if [ -n "$VENV" ]; then
  PYTHON="$VENV_PYTHON"
elif [ -n "${HERMES_PYTHON:-}" ] && [ -x "$HERMES_PYTHON" ] \
    && "$HERMES_PYTHON" -c 'import pytest' 2>/dev/null; then
  # Guard with an import check: HERMES_PYTHON may point at the RELEASE
  # venv (no pytest) when inherited from a wrapped `hermes` binary rather
  # than the devShell hook.
  PYTHON="$HERMES_PYTHON"
  echo "▶ no local venv — using Nix dev venv via HERMES_PYTHON: $PYTHON"
else
  echo "error: no virtualenv with pytest found in $REPO_ROOT/.venv or $REPO_ROOT/venv," >&2
  echo "       and HERMES_PYTHON is not a python with pytest (enter the Nix devShell or create a venv)" >&2
  if [ -n "$SKIPPED_VENVS" ]; then

fi

EXTRA_PYTEST_PLUGINS=""
if [ -f "$HOME/.hermes/pytest_live_guard.py" ]; then

  EXTRA_PYTEST_PLUGINS="pytest_live_guard"

# `env -i` forwards HOME, which is enough on POSIX. Native Windows CPython
# resolves Path.home() from USERPROFILE (or HOMEDRIVE+HOMEPATH), stdlib

# and tempfile needs TEMP/TMP. Dropping them breaks collection on native
# Windows (issues #67385, #70813). These are location variables, not
# credentials, so forwarding them keeps the isolation intent intact. Each is
# only forwarded when actually set, so POSIX runs are byte-for-byte unchanged.
WIN_ENV=()

# credential can leak" property stays auditable at a glance.
TEST_ENV=()

  HERMES_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT HERMES_TEST_FILE_RETRIES HERMES_TEST_SLICE \
  HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR HERMES_E2E_REQUIRE_TUI CI GITHUB_ACTIONS; do
  if [ -n "${!_test_var:-}" ]; then

  fi
done

# env -i: start with empty environment, opt-in only what we need.
# No credential var can leak — you'd have to explicitly add it here.
echo "▶ running per-file parallel test suite via run_tests_parallel.py"
echo "  (TZ=UTC LANG=C.UTF-8 PYTHONHASHSEED=0; clean env)"

cd "$REPO_ROOT"

# ── Pre-compile .pyc bytecode cache ─────────────────────────────────────────
# Each test file runs in its own subprocess via run_tests_parallel.py.
# Pre-building the bytecode cache once here (instead of each subprocess
# compiling on first import) avoids redundant work across ~2000 processes.
# Uses git to list tracked .py files (skips venv, node_modules, etc).

  HOME="$HOME" \

class KernelBrowser(BrowserContext):
    uses_native_tools = True
    profile_retained_on_stop = False

    def state(self, turn):
        key = self.context_key(turn)
        path = self.directory / 'kernel' / 'contexts' / (key + '.json')
        return path, self.owned_state(turn, path)

    def driver(self, turn):
        from seatbelt.context import Context
        return Context(turn.home).settings['agent_browser_executable']

    def native_task_id(self, turn):
        value = ':'.join((turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, str(turn.home.resolve()), turn.task_id))
        return 'ck-' + hashlib.sha256(value.encode()).hexdigest()[:40]

    def check_claim(self, turn, session_id):
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            owner = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelBrowser', session_id)).fetchone()
        expected = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        if not owner or tuple(owner) != expected:
            raise AccessError('This Kernel browser has no verified requester ownership.', 403)

    def endpoint_identity(self, cdp_url, session_id):
        try:
            url = urlsplit(cdp_url)
            query = parse_qs(url.query, strict_parsing=True)
            if (url.scheme != 'wss' or url.username or url.password or url.fragment or
                    not (url.hostname or '').endswith(('.kernel.sh', '.onkernel.com')) or
                    url.path != '/browser/cdp' or set(query) != {'jwt'} or len(query['jwt']) != 1):
                raise ValueError
            encoded = query['jwt'][0].split('.')[1]
            payload = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(encoded + '=' * (-len(encoded) % 4)))
            browser = payload['session']
            checks = {'session ID': browser['id'] == session_id,
                'instance hostname': isinstance(browser['fqdn'], str),
                'instance ID': isinstance(browser['instanceUuid'], str) and bool(browser['instanceUuid']),
                # Zero selects Kernel's default CDP port; an empty WebSocket
                # path similarly selects its browser endpoint.
                'CDP port': isinstance(browser['cdpPort'], int) and 0 <= browser['cdpPort'] < 65536,
                'CDP path': isinstance(browser['cdpWsPath'], str)}
            for field, valid in checks.items():
                if not valid:
                    raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control ' + field + '.', 403)
            # These URLs originate in authenticated Kernel API responses. The
            # decoded fields compare their stable routing identity; this is not
            # signature verification or an independent source of authorization.
            return (browser['id'], browser['instanceUuid'], browser['cdpPort'], browser['cdpWsPath'], browser['fqdn'])
        except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError, TypeError):
            raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control identity.', 403) from None

    def claim_endpoint(self, turn, cdp_url, session_id):
        owner = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        identity = self.endpoint_identity(cdp_url, session_id)
        # A different API session ID must not allow two owners to attach to
        # the same underlying browser instance and CDP target.
        endpoint = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(identity[1:]).encode()).hexdigest()
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
            row = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelCDP', endpoint)).fetchone()
            if row and tuple(row) != owner:
                raise AccessError('Kernel returned a browser endpoint assigned to another requester. This task is quarantined.', 403)
            db.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO browser_session_owners VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)', ('KernelCDP', endpoint, *owner))

    def browser_vault(self, turn):
        manager = getattr(self.vault, 'kernel_vault', None)
        if manager is None:
            return None
        if hasattr(manager, 'browser_vaults'):
            return validate_vault_attachments(manager.browser_vaults(turn))
        attachment = manager.browser_vault(turn)
        return validate_vault_attachments([attachment]) if attachment is not None else None

        if len(owners) > 1:

        account = self.account(team, owner, handle)
        with self.store.connection() as db:

        with self.store.connection() as db:

class KernelBrowser(BrowserContext):

    profile_retained_on_stop = False

    def state(self, turn):
        key = self.context_key(turn)
        path = self.directory / 'kernel' / 'contexts' / (key + '.json')
        return path, self.owned_state(turn, path)

    def driver(self, turn):
        from seatbelt.context import Context
        return Context(turn.home).settings['agent_browser_executable']

    def native_task_id(self, turn):
        value = ':'.join((turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, str(turn.home.resolve()), turn.task_id))
        return 'ck-' + hashlib.sha256(value.encode()).hexdigest()[:40]

    def check_claim(self, turn, session_id):
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            owner = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelBrowser', session_id)).fetchone()
        expected = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        if not owner or tuple(owner) != expected:
            raise AccessError('This Kernel browser has no verified requester ownership.', 403)

    def endpoint_identity(self, cdp_url, session_id):
        try:
            url = urlsplit(cdp_url)
            query = parse_qs(url.query, strict_parsing=True)
            if (url.scheme != 'wss' or url.username or url.password or url.fragment or
                    not (url.hostname or '').endswith(('.kernel.sh', '.onkernel.com')) or
                    url.path != '/browser/cdp' or set(query) != {'jwt'} or len(query['jwt']) != 1):
                raise ValueError
            encoded = query['jwt'][0].split('.')[1]
            payload = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(encoded + '=' * (-len(encoded) % 4)))
            browser = payload['session']
            checks = {'session ID': browser['id'] == session_id,
                'instance hostname': isinstance(browser['fqdn'], str),
                'instance ID': isinstance(browser['instanceUuid'], str) and bool(browser['instanceUuid']),
                # Zero selects Kernel's default CDP port; an empty WebSocket
                # path similarly selects its browser endpoint.
                'CDP port': isinstance(browser['cdpPort'], int) and 0 <= browser['cdpPort'] < 65536,
                'CDP path': isinstance(browser['cdpWsPath'], str)}
            for field, valid in checks.items():
                if not valid:
                    raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control ' + field + '.', 403)
            # These URLs originate in authenticated Kernel API responses. The
            # decoded fields compare their stable routing identity; this is not
            # signature verification or an independent source of authorization.
            return (browser['id'], browser['instanceUuid'], browser['cdpPort'], browser['cdpWsPath'], browser['fqdn'])
        except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError, TypeError):
            raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control identity.', 403) from None

    def claim_endpoint(self, turn, cdp_url, session_id):
        owner = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        identity = self.endpoint_identity(cdp_url, session_id)
        # A different API session ID must not allow two owners to attach to
        # the same underlying browser instance and CDP target.
        endpoint = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(identity[1:]).encode()).hexdigest()
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
            row = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelCDP', endpoint)).fetchone()
            if row and tuple(row) != owner:
                raise AccessError('Kernel returned a browser endpoint assigned to another requester. This task is quarantined.', 403)
            db.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO browser_session_owners VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)', ('KernelCDP', endpoint, *owner))

    def browser_vault(self, turn):
        manager = getattr(self.vault, 'kernel_vault', None)
        if manager is None:
            return None
        if hasattr(manager, 'browser_vaults'):
            return validate_vault_attachments(manager.browser_vaults(turn))
        attachment = manager.browser_vault(turn)
        return validate_vault_attachments([attachment]) if attachment is not None else None

        fields = {'connection_id', 'profile_name', 'handle'}
        if (not isinstance(binding, dict) or set(binding) != fields or any(
                not isinstance(value, str) or
                re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{0,199}', value) is None
                for value in binding.values())):

    def cleanup_home(self, home):

            owners = db.execute('SELECT DISTINCT team,requester FROM kernel_auth_flows WHERE home=?', (home,)).fetchall()

    def remove_account(self, team, owner, handle):
        account = self.account(team, owner, handle)

                'team=? AND account_owner=? AND account_handle=? AND state!=?', (team, owner, handle, 'deleted'))]
        for row in rows:

            self.client.delete_credential(account['credential_name'])
        with self.store.connection() as db:
            db.execute('DELETE FROM kernel_auth_accounts WHERE team=? AND owner=? AND handle=?', (team, owner, handle))

class KernelBrowser(BrowserContext):
    uses_native_tools = True
    profile_retained_on_stop = False

    def state(self, turn):
        key = self.context_key(turn)
        path = self.directory / 'kernel' / 'contexts' / (key + '.json')
        return path, self.owned_state(turn, path)

    def driver(self, turn):
        from seatbelt.context import Context
        return Context(turn.home).settings['agent_browser_executable']

    def native_task_id(self, turn):
        value = ':'.join((turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, str(turn.home.resolve()), turn.task_id))
        return 'ck-' + hashlib.sha256(value.encode()).hexdigest()[:40]

    def check_claim(self, turn, session_id):
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            owner = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelBrowser', session_id)).fetchone()
        expected = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        if not owner or tuple(owner) != expected:
            raise AccessError('This Kernel browser has no verified requester ownership.', 403)

    def endpoint_identity(self, cdp_url, session_id):
        try:
            url = urlsplit(cdp_url)
            query = parse_qs(url.query, strict_parsing=True)
            if (url.scheme != 'wss' or url.username or url.password or url.fragment or
                    not (url.hostname or '').endswith(('.kernel.sh', '.onkernel.com')) or
                    url.path != '/browser/cdp' or set(query) != {'jwt'} or len(query['jwt']) != 1):
                raise ValueError
            encoded = query['jwt'][0].split('.')[1]
            payload = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(encoded + '=' * (-len(encoded) % 4)))
            browser = payload['session']
            checks = {'session ID': browser['id'] == session_id,
                'instance hostname': isinstance(browser['fqdn'], str),
                'instance ID': isinstance(browser['instanceUuid'], str) and bool(browser['instanceUuid']),
                # Zero selects Kernel's default CDP port; an empty WebSocket
                # path similarly selects its browser endpoint.
                'CDP port': isinstance(browser['cdpPort'], int) and 0 <= browser['cdpPort'] < 65536,
                'CDP path': isinstance(browser['cdpWsPath'], str)}
            for field, valid in checks.items():
                if not valid:
                    raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control ' + field + '.', 403)
            # These URLs originate in authenticated Kernel API responses. The
            # decoded fields compare their stable routing identity; this is not
            # signature verification or an independent source of authorization.
            return (browser['id'], browser['instanceUuid'], browser['cdpPort'], browser['cdpWsPath'], browser['fqdn'])
        except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError, TypeError):
            raise AccessError('Kernel returned an unsupported browser control identity.', 403) from None

    def claim_endpoint(self, turn, cdp_url, session_id):
        owner = (turn.source.scope_id, turn.source.user_id, self.context_key(turn))
        identity = self.endpoint_identity(cdp_url, session_id)
        # A different API session ID must not allow two owners to attach to
        # the same underlying browser instance and CDP target.
        endpoint = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(identity[1:]).encode()).hexdigest()
        with self.vault.store.connection() as db:
            db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
            row = db.execute('SELECT team,requester,context FROM browser_session_owners WHERE provider=? AND session_id=?',
                ('KernelCDP', endpoint)).fetchone()
            if row and tuple(row) != owner:
                raise AccessError('Kernel returned a browser endpoint assigned to another requester. This task is quarantined.', 403)
            db.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO browser_session_owners VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)', ('KernelCDP', endpoint, *owner))

    def browser_vault(self, turn):
        manager = getattr(self.vault, 'kernel_vault', None)
        if manager is None:
            return None
        if hasattr(manager, 'browser_vaults'):
            return validate_vault_attachments(manager.browser_vaults(turn))
        attachment = manager.browser_vault(turn)
        return validate_vault_attachments([attachment]) if attachment is not None else None

    @staticmethod
    def validate_auth_binding(binding):
        if binding is None:
            return None
        fields = {'connection_id', 'profile_name', 'handle'}
        if (not isinstance(binding, dict) or set(binding) != fields or any(
                not isinstance(value, str) or
                re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{0,199}', value) is None
                for value in binding.values())):
            raise AccessError('The authenticated Kernel account binding is unsupported.', 503)
            self._cleanup(row)

    def cleanup_home(self, home):
        home = str(Path(home).resolve(strict=True))
        with self.store.connection() as db:
            owners = db.execute('SELECT DISTINCT team,requester FROM kernel_auth_flows WHERE home=?', (home,)).fetchall()
        if len(owners) > 1:
            raise AccessError('This profile has conflicting requester ownership.', 403)
        for team, requester in owners:
            self.cleanup_context(team, requester, home)

    def remove_account(self, team, owner, handle):
        account = self.account(team, owner, handle)
        with self.store.connection() as db:
            rows = [dict(row) for row in db.execute('SELECT * FROM kernel_auth_flows WHERE '
                'team=? AND account_owner=? AND account_handle=? AND state!=?', (team, owner, handle, 'deleted'))]
        for row in rows:
            self._cleanup(row)
        if account and account['credential_name']:
            self.client.delete_credential(account['credential_name'])
        with self.store.connection() as db:
            db.execute('DELETE FROM kernel_auth_accounts WHERE team=? AND owner=? AND handle=?', (team, owner, handle))

class _ResponseError(Exception):

def _argument(condition):

    return value


def _url(value, *, hosted=False, response=False):

          not any(ord(char) < 33 or ord(char) == 127 for char in value) and '\\' not in value)

# Kernel browser integration

Clanker uses the pinned [Kernel Hermes plugin](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/integrations/hermes-agent) through its authenticated native browser tools. Website browsing, shopping, login and personal-detail forms use Kernel exclusively. Foreground Python and shell work retain the separate macOS Seatbelt terminal sandbox. There is no local Chromium or Composio browser fallback.

The adapter loads the reviewed upstream `provider.py` at commit `0f5a8e80707957a40b6a1e5512b2a391671e9317` from the protected backend. It checks SHA-256 `475e97022b4015beda641028cedccbfa0333d7dea09995a1a9f99edd903a8683` before loading. The raw Kernel plugin is not separately enabled in member profiles. Its service key comes from the protected backend `.env` without changing process environment or copying the key to requester profiles.

## Browser and vault behavior

- Each workspace, requester and execution home has protected browser state; each conversation thread has its own remote browser. Native task keys also include the authenticated requester, so a common Slack task ID cannot attach two people to one browser.
- Persistent Kernel profiles are disabled. Session and underlying CDP resource claims prevent reuse across requesters. Native calls verify the live Kernel API record, remote session ID, name, stealth setting, absent profile and stable browser routing identity before control or secret fill. Kernel returns refreshed JWT capabilities; their full string is not a stable browser identifier.
- Existing private access forms, saved passwords, SMS, TOTP, personal details and invited credentials use the trusted supervisor on the verified browser. Values stay out of model arguments. Entered secrets and codes are encrypted in protected redaction state for restart recovery.
- Shared-channel private handoffs retain the originating conversation internally. Private questions, details and ordinary replies stay in the owner DM. The original channel receives separate brief milestones and a public outcome through `clanker_task_update`, without copied DM dialogue.
- Discovery checks the protected Kernel configuration, reviewed provider hash, service key and accepted host driver. It does not depend on a requester-accessible CLI wrapper or installed local Chromium. Vision is available only when its model requirements are satisfied.
- Legacy `browser_exec` and Composio browser calls are rejected before execution. Native cloud errors cannot start local Chromium. Private URL sidecars, extensions, local fallback and real desktop profiles are disabled.
- Automated payment is unavailable. Clanker prepares and verifies the cart in Kernel, then stops before Pay, Place order or any equivalent purchase commitment, including merchant-saved cards. The owner receives the merchant, items, total including fees, currency and checkout step. Card/CVV entry and payment-approval tools are not exposed. An order remains unplaced until a merchant receipt confirms it.
- `clanker_browser_stop` selects the authenticated thread itself. Deletion requires a successful delete and subsequent Kernel API 404. Uncertain creation or cleanup remains recorded and blocks reuse. Revoking invited access closes the recipient's affected browsers before cleanup is confirmed.

## Prepare and activate

The operator command previews by default and never restarts the gateway. It requires the reviewed Git checkout, private key file, configured Slack membership/vault and a prepared execution fleet. It snapshots affected configs and `.env` with mode 0600. Read its `--help` and the [operator setup](SETUP.md) before applying to a running installation.

```sh
scripts/configure-clanker-kernel-browser \
  --plugin-source /path/to/reviewed/hermes-browser-plugin \
  --key-env /path/to/private/trial/.env
```

After approval to change the live gateway, stop it with zero active agents and repeat with `--apply`. Accept the current Kernel-only execution policy using `scripts/enable-clanker-browser --home /absolute/gateway/home`, then start the gateway. Acceptance verifies the terminal boundary, removes old profile browser wrappers and stops only owned legacy local browser processes. New execution profiles use the protected Kernel provider automatically.

Use the returned rollback snapshot with `--restore-backup /absolute/snapshot/path` to preview restoration; add `--apply` only for a reviewed compatible Kernel configuration. Historical Composio records and backups are retained as evidence, not an active browser option. Removing the integration does not prove deletion of old remote Composio resources.

## India residential proxy

`scripts/configure-kernel-residential-proxy` previews with authenticated reads only. It checks the organization's managed-proxy entitlement and the complete proxy list. It adopts the configured proxy ID or the unique name `clanker-india-residential`; the accepted policy is residential egress in India, without extra location selectors or bypass hosts. Credentials remain in the protected backend `.env`.

```sh
scripts/configure-kernel-residential-proxy --home /absolute/gateway/home
```

For `--apply`, first stop the owning gateway completely with zero active agents. Apply creates the named proxy only if absent, checks its health, verifies the exact available remote resource, and atomically adds `proxy: {id, type: "residential", country: "IN"}` to the protected Kernel config. It snapshots the previous config with mode 0600 and preserves the other settings. It never restarts the gateway, deletes a proxy/browser or sends Slack messages. `--proxy-id ID` selects an existing India residential proxy explicitly.

If a create request loses its acknowledgement, a protected dispatch marker blocks another creation. Rerunning can recover only the exact unique named proxy and then pins its ID; if it is absent or ambiguous, investigate the marker instead of repeating creation. Use the returned `--restore-backup /absolute/snapshot/path` to preview a SHA-checked config rollback; add `--apply` while the gateway is stopped to restore it. Restoration leaves the remote proxy intact.

Restart through the existing gateway procedure after applying. Every browser must match the current protected routing policy before control or private fill; an old default-egress browser is blocked when residential routing is configured. Stop and reopen an incompatible browser in the same task to apply the current policy. A confirmed expired remote browser can be recreated there automatically. Changing Slack threads is not required, and changing the backend setting does not silently move an existing remote browser. Runtime checks also require the residential proxy's exact ID, India routing and availability. Proxy health alone does not prove that a retailer permits the session or that ordering succeeds.

## Verification

`scripts/kernel-clanker-smoke --help` describes the explicit live check. It stages a fresh isolated backend, reads the existing private trial key, and opens public Example Domain browsers for two synthetic owners through the real model-tool dispatcher. It checks owner separation and A → B → A reattachment, fills a synthetic password in a DOM-only fixture without submitting anything, verifies redaction, and confirms deletion. It never sends a Slack message or uses an actual website account.

Fixtures cover vault storage and handlers for password/SMS/TOTP/personal/invited fills, revocation, cleanup failures, endpoint collisions, metadata tampering, native schemas and restart redaction. `verification/probes/test_kernel_only_routing.py` checks discovery, stale-tool denial, protected driver readiness, terminal availability and owner-only payment guidance. `verification/probes/clanker_kernel_discovery_profile_probe.py` checks real A → B → A plugin discovery and fixture dispatch without provider requests or browser launches.

Earlier integration evidence is recorded in `verification/evidence/2026-10-08-kernel-integration.md`; historical local-checkout checks do not describe the current browser flow. Retailer login, Add to Bag and ordering need fresh website-specific evidence. Public/synthetic probes and proxy health do not establish that Apple, Blinkit or Instamart checkout succeeds.

Website browsing, shopping, login and personal-detail forms use Kernel exclusively. Foreground Python and shell work retain the separate macOS Seatbelt terminal sandbox. The adapter loads the reviewed upstream `provider.py` at commit `0f5a8e80707957a40b6a1e5512b2a391671e9317` from the protected backend. It checks SHA-256 `475e97022b4015beda641028cedccbfa0333d7dea09995a1a9f99edd903a8683` before loading. The raw Kernel plugin is not separately enabled in member profiles. Its service key comes from the protected backend `.env` without changing process environment or copying the key to requester profiles.

## Browser and vault behavior

- Each workspace, requester and execution home has protected browser state; each conversation thread has its own remote browser. Native task keys also include the authenticated requester, so a common Slack task ID cannot attach two people to one browser.
- Persistent Kernel profiles are disabled. Session and underlying CDP resource claims prevent reuse across requesters. Native calls verify the live Kernel API record, remote session ID, name, stealth setting, absent profile and stable browser routing identity before control or secret fill. Kernel returns refreshed JWT capabilities; their full string is not a stable browser identifier.
- Existing private access forms, saved passwords, SMS, TOTP, personal details and invited credentials use the trusted supervisor on the verified browser. Values stay out of model arguments. Entered secrets and codes are encrypted in protected redaction state for restart recovery.
- Shared-channel private handoffs retain the originating conversation internally. Private questions, details and ordinary replies stay in the owner DM. The original channel receives separate brief milestones and a public outcome through `clanker_task_update`, without copied DM dialogue.
- Discovery checks the protected Kernel configuration, reviewed provider hash, service key and accepted host driver. It does not depend on a requester-accessible CLI wrapper or installed local Chromium. Vision is available only when its model requirements are satisfied.
- Legacy `browser_exec` and Composio browser calls are rejected before execution. Native cloud errors cannot start local Chromium. Private URL sidecars, extensions, local fallback and real desktop profiles are disabled.
- Automated payment is unavailable. Clanker prepares and verifies the cart in Kernel, then stops before Pay, Place order or any equivalent purchase commitment, including merchant-saved cards. The owner receives the merchant, items, total including fees, currency and checkout step. Card/CVV entry and payment-approval tools are not exposed. An order remains unplaced until a merchant receipt confirms it.
- `clanker_browser_stop` selects the authenticated thread itself. Deletion requires a successful delete and subsequent Kernel API 404. Uncertain creation or cleanup remains recorded and blocks reuse. Revoking invited access closes the recipient's affected browsers before cleanup is confirmed.

It never restarts the gateway, deletes a proxy/browser or sends Slack messages. `--proxy-id ID` selects an existing India residential proxy explicitly.

Apply creates the named proxy only if absent, checks its health, verifies the exact available remote resource, and atomically adds `proxy: {id, type: "residential", country: "IN"}` to the protected Kernel config. It snapshots the previous config with mode 0600 and preserves the other settings. It never restarts the gateway, deletes a proxy/browser or sends Slack messages. `--proxy-id ID` selects an existing India residential proxy explicitly.

If a create request loses its acknowledgement, a protected dispatch marker blocks another creation. Rerunning can recover only the exact unique named proxy and then pins its ID; if it is absent or ambiguous, investigate the marker instead of repeating creation. Use the returned `--restore-backup /absolute/snapshot/path` to preview a SHA-checked config rollback; add `--apply` while the gateway is stopped to restore it. Restoration leaves the remote proxy intact.

Restart through the existing gateway procedure after applying. Every browser must match the current protected routing policy before control or private fill; an old default-egress browser is blocked when residential routing is configured. Stop and reopen an incompatible browser in the same task to apply the current policy. A confirmed expired remote browser can be recreated there automatically. Changing Slack threads is not required, and changing the backend setting does not silently move an existing remote browser. Runtime checks also require the residential proxy's exact ID, India routing and availability. Proxy health alone does not prove that a retailer permits the session or that ordering succeeds.

## Verification

`scripts/kernel-clanker-smoke --help` describes the explicit live check. It stages a fresh isolated backend, reads the existing private trial key, and opens public Example Domain browsers for two synthetic owners through the real model-tool dispatcher. It checks owner separation and A → B → A reattachment, fills a synthetic password in a DOM-only fixture without submitting anything, verifies redaction, and confirms deletion. It never sends a Slack message or uses an actual website account.

Fixtures cover vault storage and handlers for password/SMS/TOTP/personal/invited fills, revocation, cleanup failures, endpoint collisions, metadata tampering, native schemas and restart redaction. `verification/probes/test_kernel_only_routing.py` checks discovery, stale-tool denial, protected driver readiness, terminal availability and owner-only payment guidance. `verification/probes/clanker_kernel_discovery_profile_probe.py` checks real A → B → A plugin discovery and fixture dispatch without provider requests or browser launches.

Earlier integration evidence is recorded in `verification/evidence/2026-10-08-kernel-integration.md`; historical local-checkout checks do not describe the current browser flow. Retailer login, Add to Bag and ordering need fresh website-specific evidence. Public/synthetic probes and proxy health do not establish that Apple, Blinkit or Instamart checkout succeeds.

## Implementing the pattern with Kernel's Managed Auth

Kernel Managed Auth implements these principles through a connection, a login session, and a browser profile. The connection stores authorization for one domain without placing credentials inside the agent loop. Kernel encrypts credentials at rest with per-organization keys, never returns them through API responses, never writes them to logs, and never passes them to an LLM.

First, create a Managed Auth Connection and attach it to the profile that will represent the agent. If the profile does not exist, Kernel creates it. Each connection targets one domain. To constrain where credentials may be entered as the flow moves across redirects, set `allowed_domains` — when that field is omitted or empty, credential entry is not restricted to the primary domain. Common SSO provider domains such as Google, Microsoft, Okta, Auth0, and GitHub are allowed automatically and do not need to be listed.

Next, start a login session for the connection and follow its state until it reports `SUCCESS`. ## Running one agent identity across multiple tools

A single Kernel browser profile can hold multiple Managed Auth connections, each targeting one domain. You can attach a CRM connection and a procurement portal connection to the same profile, then launch one browser where the agent is authenticated to both tools at once.

The profile serves as the agent's persistent identity container. When the agent opens either site, the browser presents that site's cookies under normal browser origin rules while the LLM receives only page content and available actions. Because everything in a profile shares one cookie jar, the profile — not the individual connection — is the boundary to reason about: give distinct agent identities distinct profiles.

Profiles load read-only unless you pass `save_changes: true`, and only one writer is safe at a time, since each save replaces the profile's stored state wholesale.

Adding another tool repeats the connection step without changing your agent logic. Each site keeps its own login and re-authentication lifecycle, so a change to one domain does not require rebuilding authentication for the others.

# Hermes Agent - Development Guide

Instructions for AI coding assistants and developers working on the hermes-agent codebase.
This root file holds only what applies everywhere. Each area has its own `AGENTS.md` (aim for
~8k chars; `agent/subdirectory_hints.py` delivers up to 32k and truncates head/tail with a warning
past that); see the **routing table** at the end and read the area file before editing in that area.

**Never give up on the right solution.**

## What Hermes Is

Hermes is a personal AI agent that runs the same agent core across a CLI, a messaging
gateway (Telegram, Discord, Slack, ~20 platforms), a TUI, and an Electron desktop app. It
learns across sessions (memory + skills), delegates to subagents, runs scheduled jobs, and
drives a real terminal and browser. It is extended primarily through **plugins and skills**,
not by growing the core.

Two invariants shape almost every design decision and are the lens for reviewing any change:

- **Per-conversation prompt caching is sacred.** A long-lived conversation reuses a cached
  prefix every turn. Anything that mutates past context, swaps toolsets, reloads memories, or
  rebuilds the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates that cache and multiplies the user's
  cost. We do not do it; the ONE exception is context compression. Slash commands that mutate
  system-prompt state (skills, tools, memory) must be **cache-aware**: default to deferred
  invalidation (takes effect next session) with an opt-in `--now` flag (`/skills install --now`
  is the canonical pattern).
- **The core is a narrow waist; capability lives at the edges.** Every model tool is sent on
  every API call, so the bar for a new *core* tool is high. New capability should arrive as a
  CLI command + skill, a service-gated tool, or a plugin — not as core surface.

## Contribution Rubric — What We Want / What We Don't

The project's intent layer. It serves humans aiming a contribution AND the automated triage
sweeper, which may only close on `implemented_on_main`, `cannot_reproduce`, or `incoherent`.
Taste-based "out of scope" closes are a human maintainer's call; the sweeper's job is to
recognize design intent and *avoid wrongly closing a legitimate contribution*.

Read the balance right: Hermes ships a **lot**. Most merges are bug fixes to reported
behavior, and the product surface (platforms, providers, models, desktop/TUI features)
expands aggressively on purpose. The restraint below targets the **core agent + model tool
schema**, the one place where every addition is paid for on every API call. "Smallest
footprint" governs *how a capability is wired into the core*, not whether the product may
grow: expansive at the edges, conservative at the waist.

### What we want

- **Fix real bugs, well.** Reproduce the symptom on current `main`, point to the exact line
  where it manifests, and fix the whole bug class — sibling call paths included.
- **Expand reach at the edges.** New adapters, channels, providers, models, desktop/TUI/
  dashboard features land routinely, including large ones — as long as they integrate with
  the existing setup/config UX (`hermes tools`, `hermes setup`, auto-install) rather than
  bolting on a raw env var.
- **Refactor god-files into clean modules.** Huge mechanical `+N/-N` extraction PRs are
  wanted work. "Every line traces to the request" applies to *feature* PRs; a declared
  refactor's request IS the extraction.
- **Keep the core narrow.** Prefer, in order: extend existing code → CLI command + skill →
  service-gated tool (`check_fn`) → plugin → MCP server in the catalog → new core tool (last
  resort). See the Footprint Ladder.
- **Extend, don't duplicate.** Check whether existing infrastructure covers the use case
  before adding a module/manager/hook. When 3+ open PRs integrate the same *category*
  (memory backends, providers, notifiers), design an ABC + orchestrator, wrap the existing
  built-in as the first provider, and turn the competing PRs into plugins against it.
- **Behavior contracts over snapshots.** Tests assert how two pieces of data relate, never
  freeze a current value (see Testing).
- **E2E validation, not just green unit mocks.** Anything touching resolution chains, config
  propagation, security boundaries, remote backends, or file/network I/O must exercise the
  real path with real imports against a temp `HERMES_HOME` — two of them (A→B→A) when the
  change touches profile scope. Mocks hide integration bugs.
- **Cache-, alternation-, and invariant-safe.** Preserve prompt caching, strict role
  alternation (never two same-role messages in a row; never a synthetic user message injected
  mid-loop), and a system prompt byte-stable for the life of a conversation.
- **Contributor credit preserved.** Salvage external work by cherry-picking (rebase-merge) so
  authorship survives; build on top rather than reimplementing.

### What we don't want (rejected even when well-built)

- **Speculative infrastructure.** Hooks/callbacks/extension points with no concrete consumer.
  Adding a hook is easy; removing one after plugins depend on it is hard. A hook with a real,
  stated use case is NOT speculative even if the consumer ships separately.
- **New `HERMES_*` env vars for non-secret config.** `.env` is for secrets only. Behavioral
  settings (timeouts, thresholds, flags, display prefs) go in `config.yaml`; bridge to an
  internal env var in code if the mechanism needs one. Reject "set X in your .env" docs
  unless X is a credential.
- **A new core tool when terminal + file (or a skill) already do the job.** If the only
  barrier is file visibility on a remote backend, fix the mount, not the toolset.
- **Lazy-reading escape hatches on instructional tools.** No `offset`/`limit` pagination on
  tools that load content the agent must read fully (skills, prompts, playbooks) — models
  read page 1 and skip the rest.
- **"Fixes" that destroy the feature they secure.** Read the original intent
  (`git log -p -S`) before restricting behavior; find a fix that preserves the feature.

# Hermes Agent - Development Guide

Instructions for AI coding assistants and developers working on the hermes-agent codebase.
This root file holds only what applies everywhere. Each area has its own `AGENTS.md` (aim for
~8k chars; `agent/subdirectory_hints.py` delivers up to 32k and truncates head/tail with a warning
past that); see the **routing table** at the end and read the area file before editing in that area.

**Never give up on the right solution.**

## What Hermes Is

Hermes is a personal AI agent that runs the same agent core across a CLI, a messaging
gateway (Telegram, Discord, Slack, ~20 platforms), a TUI, and an Electron desktop app. It
learns across sessions (memory + skills), delegates to subagents, runs scheduled jobs, and
drives a real terminal and browser. It is extended primarily through **plugins and skills**,
not by growing the core.

Two invariants shape almost every design decision and are the lens for reviewing any change:

- **Per-conversation prompt caching is sacred.** A long-lived conversation reuses a cached
  prefix every turn. Anything that mutates past context, swaps toolsets, reloads memories, or
  rebuilds the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates that cache and multiplies the user's
  cost. We do not do it; the ONE exception is context compression. Slash commands that mutate
  system-prompt state (skills, tools, memory) must be **cache-aware**: default to deferred
  invalidation (takes effect next session) with an opt-in `--now` flag (`/skills install --now`
  is the canonical pattern).
- **The core is a narrow waist; capability lives at the edges.** Every model tool is sent on
  every API call, so the bar for a new *core* tool is high. New capability should arrive as a
  CLI command + skill, a service-gated tool, or a plugin — not as core surface.

## Contribution Rubric — What We Want / What We Don't

The project's intent layer. It serves humans aiming a contribution AND the automated triage
sweeper, which may only close on `implemented_on_main`, `cannot_reproduce`, or `incoherent`.
Taste-based "out of scope" closes are a human maintainer's call; the sweeper's job is to
recognize design intent and *avoid wrongly closing a legitimate contribution*.

Read the balance right: Hermes ships a **lot**. Most merges are bug fixes to reported
behavior, and the product surface (platforms, providers, models, desktop/TUI features)
expands aggressively on purpose. The restraint below targets the **core agent + model tool
schema**, the one place where every addition is paid for on every API call. "Smallest
footprint" governs *how a capability is wired into the core*, not whether the product may
grow: expansive at the edges, conservative at the waist.

### What we want

- **Fix real bugs, well.** Reproduce the symptom on current `main`, point to the exact line
  where it manifests, and fix the whole bug class — sibling call paths included.
- **Expand reach at the edges.** New adapters, channels, providers, models, desktop/TUI/
  dashboard features land routinely, including large ones — as long as they integrate with
  the existing setup/config UX (`hermes tools`, `hermes setup`, auto-install) rather than
  bolting on a raw env var.
- **Refactor god-files into clean modules.** Huge mechanical `+N/-N` extraction PRs are
  wanted work. "Every line traces to the request" applies to *feature* PRs; a declared
  refactor's request IS the extraction.
- **Keep the core narrow.** Prefer, in order: extend existing code → CLI command + skill →
  service-gated tool (`check_fn`) → plugin → MCP server in the catalog → new core tool (last
  resort). See the Footprint Ladder.
- **Extend, don't duplicate.** Check whether existing infrastructure covers the use case
  before adding a module/manager/hook. When 3+ open PRs integrate the same *category*
  (memory backends, providers, notifiers), design an ABC + orchestrator, wrap the existing
  built-in as the first provider, and turn the competing PRs into plugins against it.
- **Behavior contracts over snapshots.** Tests assert how two pieces of data relate, never
  freeze a current value (see Testing).
- **E2E validation, not just green unit mocks.** Anything touching resolution chains, config
  propagation, security boundaries, remote backends, or file/network I/O must exercise the
  real path with real imports against a temp `HERMES_HOME` — two of them (A→B→A) when the
  change touches profile scope. Mocks hide integration bugs.
- **Cache-, alternation-, and invariant-safe.** Preserve prompt caching, strict role
  alternation (never two same-role messages in a row; never a synthetic user message injected
  mid-loop), and a system prompt byte-stable for the life of a conversation.
- **Contributor credit preserved.** Salvage external work by cherry-picking (rebase-merge) so
  authorship survives; build on top rather than reimplementing.

### What we don't want (rejected even when well-built)

- **Speculative infrastructure.** Hooks/callbacks/extension points with no concrete consumer.
  Adding a hook is easy; removing one after plugins depend on it is hard. A hook with a real,
  stated use case is NOT speculative even if the consumer ships separately.
- **New `HERMES_*` env vars for non-secret config.** `.env` is for secrets only. Behavioral
  settings (timeouts, thresholds, flags, display prefs) go in `config.yaml`; bridge to an
  internal env var in code if the mechanism needs one. Reject "set X in your .env" docs
  unless X is a credential.
- **A new core tool when terminal + file (or a skill) already do the job.** If the only
  barrier is file visibility on a remote backend, fix the mount, not the toolset.
- **Lazy-reading escape hatches on instructional tools.** No `offset`/`limit` pagination on
  tools that load content the agent must read fully (skills, prompts, playbooks) — models
  read page 1 and skip the rest.
- **"Fixes" that destroy the feature they secure.** Read the original intent
  (`git log -p -S`) before restricting behavior; find a fix that preserves the feature.

# Hermes Agent - Development Guide

Instructions for AI coding assistants and developers working on the hermes-agent codebase.
This root file holds only what applies everywhere. Each area has its own `AGENTS.md` (aim for
~8k chars; `agent/subdirectory_hints.py` delivers up to 32k and truncates head/tail with a warning
past that); see the **routing table** at the end and read the area file before editing in that area.

**Never give up on the right solution.**

## What Hermes Is

Hermes is a personal AI agent that runs the same agent core across a CLI, a messaging
gateway (Telegram, Discord, Slack, ~20 platforms), a TUI, and an Electron desktop app. It
learns across sessions (memory + skills), delegates to subagents, runs scheduled jobs, and
drives a real terminal and browser. It is extended primarily through **plugins and skills**,
not by growing the core.

Two invariants shape almost every design decision and are the lens for reviewing any change:

- **Per-conversation prompt caching is sacred.** A long-lived conversation reuses a cached
  prefix every turn. Anything that mutates past context, swaps toolsets, reloads memories, or
  rebuilds the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates that cache and multiplies the user's
  cost. We do not do it; the ONE exception is context compression. Slash commands that mutate
  system-prompt state (skills, tools, memory) must be **cache-aware**: default to deferred
  invalidation (takes effect next session) with an opt-in `--now` flag (`/skills install --now`
  is the canonical pattern).
- **The core is a narrow waist; capability lives at the edges.** Every model tool is sent on
  every API call, so the bar for a new *core* tool is high. New capability should arrive as a
  CLI command + skill, a service-gated tool, or a plugin — not as core surface.

## Contribution Rubric — What We Want / What We Don't

The project's intent layer. It serves humans aiming a contribution AND the automated triage
sweeper, which may only close on `implemented_on_main`, `cannot_reproduce`, or `incoherent`.
Taste-based "out of scope" closes are a human maintainer's call; the sweeper's job is to
recognize design intent and *avoid wrongly closing a legitimate contribution*.

Read the balance right: Hermes ships a **lot**. Most merges are bug fixes to reported
behavior, and the product surface (platforms, providers, models, desktop/TUI features)
expands aggressively on purpose. The restraint below targets the **core agent + model tool
schema**, the one place where every addition is paid for on every API call. "Smallest
footprint" governs *how a capability is wired into the core*, not whether the product may
grow: expansive at the edges, conservative at the waist.

### What we want

- **Fix real bugs, well.** Reproduce the symptom on current `main`, point to the exact line
  where it manifests, and fix the whole bug class — sibling call paths included.
- **Expand reach at the edges.** New adapters, channels, providers, models, desktop/TUI/
  dashboard features land routinely, including large ones — as long as they integrate with
  the existing setup/config UX (`hermes tools`, `hermes setup`, auto-install) rather than
  bolting on a raw env var.
- **Refactor god-files into clean modules.** Huge mechanical `+N/-N` extraction PRs are
  wanted work. "Every line traces to the request" applies to *feature* PRs; a declared
  refactor's request IS the extraction.
- **Keep the core narrow.** Prefer, in order: extend existing code → CLI command + skill →
  service-gated tool (`check_fn`) → plugin → MCP server in the catalog → new core tool (last
  resort). See the Footprint Ladder.
- **Extend, don't duplicate.** Check whether existing infrastructure covers the use case
  before adding a module/manager/hook. When 3+ open PRs integrate the same *category*
  (memory backends, providers, notifiers), design an ABC + orchestrator, wrap the existing
  built-in as the first provider, and turn the competing PRs into plugins against it.
- **Behavior contracts over snapshots.** Tests assert how two pieces of data relate, never
  freeze a current value (see Testing).
- **E2E validation, not just green unit mocks.** Anything touching resolution chains, config
  propagation, security boundaries, remote backends, or file/network I/O must exercise the
  real path with real imports against a temp `HERMES_HOME` — two of them (A→B→A) when the
  change touches profile scope. Mocks hide integration bugs.
- **Cache-, alternation-, and invariant-safe.** Preserve prompt caching, strict role
  alternation (never two same-role messages in a row; never a synthetic user message injected
  mid-loop), and a system prompt byte-stable for the life of a conversation.
- **Contributor credit preserved.** Salvage external work by cherry-picking (rebase-merge) so
  authorship survives; build on top rather than reimplementing.

### What we don't want (rejected even when well-built)

- **Speculative infrastructure.** Hooks/callbacks/extension points with no concrete consumer.
  Adding a hook is easy; removing one after plugins depend on it is hard. A hook with a real,
  stated use case is NOT speculative even if the consumer ships separately.
- **New `HERMES_*` env vars for non-secret config.** `.env` is for secrets only. Behavioral
  settings (timeouts, thresholds, flags, display prefs) go in `config.yaml`; bridge to an
  internal env var in code if the mechanism needs one. Reject "set X in your .env" docs
  unless X is a credential.
- **A new core tool when terminal + file (or a skill) already do the job.** If the only
  barrier is file visibility on a remote backend, fix the mount, not the toolset.
- **Lazy-reading escape hatches on instructional tools.** No `offset`/`limit` pagination on
  tools that load content the agent must read fully (skills, prompts, playbooks) — models
  read page 1 and skip the rest.
- **"Fixes" that destroy the feature they secure.** Read the original intent
  (`git log -p -S`) before restricting behavior; find a fix that preserves the feature.

L21: Choose how your browser agents authenticate and reuse signed-in sessions
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: most useful browser workflows begin behind a login. KERNEL gives you two ways to authenticate browser agents without returning stored sensitive values through the api or putting them in your agent prompt: control the workflow yourself and Fill from Vault, or delegate the login and session lifecycle to Managed Auth.
L25: Fill from Vault is the recommended approach if you require greater visibility and control over the authentication experience, while Managed Auth is preferred if you would like KERNEL to handle the login lifecycle on your behalf.
L26: ##
L27:

L30: Choose an auth approach
L31: 
L32: ## Fill from Vault
L33: 
L34: control the login workflow
L35: ## Managed Auth
L36: 
L37: delegate the login lifecycle
L38:  | Fill from Vault  | Managed Auth
L39: --- | --- | ---
L40: login orchestration  | your application or agent owns navigation, submission, and response handling  | KERNEL runs the login flow and requests user input when needed
L41: where login happens  | in your agent’s current browser session  | in a separate browser session managed by KERNEL
L42: credential collection  | KERNEL-hosted collection form or your trusted backend  | Managed Auth credential, Hosted UI, React component, or programmatic flow
L43: credential filling  | your application invokes `fill` with field names and selectors  | KERNEL fills credentials as part of the managed login flow
L44: session state  | your workflow can save the resulting state to a profile  | saved to a reusable profile
L45: ongoing recovery  | your workflow decides when and how to authenticate again  | health checks and eligible automatic reauthentication attempts; your application brings the user back when input is required
L46: ##
L47: 
L48: cite4†​ L49: 
L50: Common use cases
L51: ###
L52: 
L53: cite5†​ L54: 
L55: Use Fill from Vault
L56:   * an authentication prompt can appear in the middle of a longer workflow, in the same browser session.
L57:   * your product needs to control when and how it asks for credentials.
L58:   * your application or agent must own navigation, submission, and recovery.
L59: one common use case is an ai assistant doing work on behalf of an end user. with Fill from Vault, the agent can login as the user to complete tasks on gated websites. your application or agent controls credential collection and completes the login in its current browser session.
L60: ###
L61: 
L62: cite6†​ L63: 
L64: Use Managed Auth
L65: 
L66:   * the automation runs unattended or signs in repeatedly.
L67:   * you want KERNEL to navigate common login, sso, and mfa flows.
L68:   * you want health checks and eligible automatic reauthentication.
L69: one common use case is recurring website qa on a set of known sites. KERNEL handles the login flow and attempts eligible automatic recovery before the automation begins. the automation can start testing on websites without needing to login.

Page scripts, extensions, developer tools, and an agent with unrestricted browser access can read them after fill. Use the narrowest browser permissions that your workflow supports, and only attach a vault to sessions authorized to use all of its items.

L83: cite9†Profiles persist cookies and local storage between browser sessions. Managed Auth saves successful logins to a profile automatically. A workflow using Fill from Vault can also save the resulting browser state to a profile when it needs to reuse that session.

"""Kernel-hosted login and explicitly selected authenticated profiles.

Only account/flow references live here. Kernel collects credentials and fresh
codes, orchestrates login, and saves the profile. No DOM login writer is used.
"""
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import secrets
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

from .store import AccessError
from .kernel_store import _origin


class ManagedAuth:
    def __init__(self, service):
        from cloud_browser.kernel_auth_client import KernelAuthClient
        self.service = service
        self.store = service.store
        self.client = KernelAuthClient(service.cloud_browser.client)
        with self.store.connection() as db:
            had_bindings = db.execute("SELECT 1 FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' "
                "AND name='kernel_auth_bindings'").fetchone() is not None
            db.executescript('''
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS kernel_auth_accounts (
                  team TEXT NOT NULL, owner TEXT NOT NULL, handle TEXT NOT NULL,
                  origin TEXT NOT NULL, created REAL NOT NULL, credential_name TEXT,
                  PRIMARY KEY(team,owner,handle));
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS kernel_auth_flows (
                  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, team TEXT NOT NULL, requester TEXT NOT NULL,
                  home TEXT NOT NULL, thread TEXT NOT NULL, account_owner TEXT NOT NULL,
                  account_handle TEXT NOT NULL, handle TEXT NOT NULL, binding TEXT NOT NULL,
                  origin TEXT NOT NULL, profile_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
                  connection_id TEXT UNIQUE, request_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
                  state TEXT NOT NULL, event_id TEXT, proxy_id TEXT,
                  created REAL NOT NULL, updated REAL NOT NULL, flow_expires_at TEXT, flow_digest TEXT);

+# Reuse successful owned logins across private DM threads
+
+## Evidence
+
+The Slack CLI authenticated as Clanker (`U0C5Z1ZQHQX`) in workspace
+`T0C6J1XCDE0`. `conversations.info` confirmed that linked conversation
+`D0C6EAXPKEE` is the DM with Tanishq (`U0C688SF7DZ`). Both
+`conversations.replies` reads reached the final page: the
+[original iCloud mail task](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/D0C6EAXPKEE/p1791494671575999)
+contained its parent and three replies; the
+[Gouri follow-up](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/D0C6EAXPKEE/p1791495668195229)
+contained its parent and two replies. The original task reported a completed mail
+search, and the follow-up requested another sign-in roughly two minutes later.
+
+Read-only inspection of the exact local auth records found the original flow
+already `deleted` with its request `cancelled`, six seconds before the completion
+reply. The next thread had a separate `pending` login. Both belonged to the
+requester's canonical private profile and the same owned iCloud account. The
